interactive.title: The mirror bench
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Fourteen small screens about a flat mirror. Most look down on it from above. The periscope screens look from the side. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. The mirror is a straight line with a handle that turns it. On the early screens a torch shines a beam at it. Later a small lamp and an eye stand in front of it. The lamp is the object. You can drag either one. Light is drawn as rays, straight lines with arrows. Where a ray strikes the mirror, a thin line stands at 90° to the surface. That is the normal. Both angles are measured from it and labelled. Here is the rule the picture follows. A ray leaves the mirror at the same angle to the normal as it arrives. The eye cannot tell that the light bounced, so it traces each ray straight back. Dashed lines carry the reflected rays back behind the mirror. Because the angles are equal, each traced-back line is the arriving ray flipped across the mirror. So every one from one point passes through the same spot. That spot is the image, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. No light travels along the dashed lines, so the image is seen only from where reflected light arrives. Drag the eye past the mirror's end, and no ray reaches it. A note then says the image cannot be seen from here. A switch adds a second mirror at 45° below the first. That makes a periscope. A readout adds up the folded path. A readout that would give a puzzle's answer shows "?" until the answer is checked. Any row of readouts wraps onto two lines on a phone. The screens, in order. Screen 1, do, Which way?: a torch beam striking the mirror at a slant, with four paths drawn faintly away from the mirror. "A torch beam strikes a flat mirror at a slant. Which way does it leave?" Choices, in a column: At the same slant, tipped the other way (right); Straight back along the beam; Straight out, square to the mirror; Along the mirror's surface. Hint on Straight back along the beam: "That happens only when the beam strikes square on." Hint on Straight out, square to the mirror: "Only a beam that arrives square on leaves square." Hint on Along the mirror's surface: "A mirror sends light back off it, not along it." Read: "A torch beam strikes a flat mirror at a slant. Which way does it leave?" Why: a mirror sends light off at the same slant it arrives at. It leaves on the other side of the line square to the mirror. After Check the beam plays and reflects. Screen 2, show, Equal angles: the torch, the mirror and the normal where the beam strikes, both angles labelled. Words: "Where the ray strikes, draw a line at 90° to the mirror. That line is the normal. Both angles are measured from it. The ray arrives at the angle of incidence. It leaves at the angle of reflection. The two are equal." Then "Drag the torch." Read: "Wherever the torch points, the beam arrives and leaves at equal angles to the normal. Here they are 35° and 35°." Still: the torch at 35° to the normal. Screen 3, do, typed, From the normal: a beam striking the mirror, its angle to the surface labelled 25°, the normal drawn and the angle of reflection showing "?". "A beam strikes a mirror at 25° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection?" A typed answer: 65°, a whole number. Slips: 25°, "That is measured from the surface. Both angles are measured from the normal."; 115°, "That adds 90°. Take 25° from 90° instead." Hint: "Measure from the normal, at 90° to the surface." Read: "A beam strikes a mirror at 25° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection?" Why: the normal is at 90° to the surface. So the beam arrives 90 − 25 = 65° from the normal. It leaves at the same 65° on the other side. The angle shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 4, show, Turn the mirror: the torch held still and the mirror turned by its handle, the old and new reflected beams both drawn. The normal turns with the mirror, and both angles to it are labelled. Words: "With the torch still, the reflected beam turns twice as far as the mirror. Turn the mirror 10°, and the normal turns 10° with it. So the angle of incidence goes from 30° to 40°. The angle of reflection does too. The angle between the arriving and leaving beams is the two added. So it changes by 20°." Then "Turn the mirror by its handle." Read: "With the torch held still, turning the mirror 10° turns the reflected beam 20°. Both angles to the normal go from 30° to 40°." Still: the mirror turned 10°. Screen 5, do, typed, Follow the target: a torch beam reflecting off the mirror onto a target, which then slides round. "A torch beam reflects off a mirror onto a target. The target moves 30° round the mirror. How far must you turn the mirror to keep the beam on it?" A typed answer: 15°, a whole number. Slips: 30°, "Turning the mirror turns the beam twice as far."; 60°, "The mirror turns half as far as the beam, not twice." Hint: "The beam turns twice as far as the mirror." Read: "A torch beam reflects off a mirror onto a target. The target moves 30° round the mirror. How far must you turn the mirror to keep the beam on it?" Why: turning the mirror by an angle turns the beam by twice that angle. So the mirror turns half of 30°. That is 15°. Turned 15°, the mirror puts the beam back on the target. After Check a handle appears, and a line above the picture says "Now turn the mirror by its handle onto the target." Turned 15°, the beam lands on the target and a label says "on target". Screen 6, show, Where the image sits: the lamp 40 cm in front of the mirror and the eye off to one side, with the ray from lamp to mirror to eye and its dashed line back. Words: "The image sits as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Your eye cannot tell that light bounced. It traces each ray straight back. Because the angles are equal, each traced-back line is the arriving ray flipped across the mirror. So they all pass through one spot, the lamp flipped across the mirror. That spot is the image." Then "Drag the eye." Read: "As the eye moves, the ray bounces off a different spot on the mirror. Its dashed line back still ends at the same image. The image is 40 cm behind the mirror, and the lamp is 40 cm in front." Still: the eye to one side of the lamp. Screen 7, do, Find the image: the lamp, the mirror and the eye off to one side, no rays drawn. "Where does this eye see the lamp's image?" Choices, in a column: Behind the mirror, straight across from the lamp, as far back (right); On the mirror's surface, where the ray bounces; On the eye's straight line through the lamp; It moves whenever the eye moves. Hint on On the mirror's surface: "Trace the ray into the eye straight back. It carries on past the mirror." Hint on On the eye's straight line through the lamp: "That line ends at the lamp itself. Trace back the reflected ray instead." Hint on It moves whenever the eye moves: "Every eye's traced-back ray passes through the same spot." Read: "A lamp stands in front of a mirror. An eye looks in from one side. Where does this eye see the lamp's image?" Why: the eye traces the reflected ray straight back. The angles are equal, so that line passes through one spot for any eye. The spot is straight across the mirror from the lamp. It is as far behind as the lamp is in front. After Check the ray and its dashed line back appear. Screen 8, show, A worked example: a person standing 1.5 m in front of a wall mirror, with their image behind it. Words: "Stand 1.5 m in front of a mirror. Your image is 1.5 m behind it. So it looks 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0 m away from you." Screen 9, do, typed, Step closer: the person 1.2 m from the mirror, an arrow showing a step of 0.4 m towards it. "You stand 1.2 m from a mirror, then step 0.4 m closer. How far away does your image look now?" A typed answer: 1.6 m, to one decimal place. Slips: 2.0 m, "Your image steps closer too."; 0.8 m, "That is your distance from the mirror. Add the image's distance behind it."; 2.4 m, "That was before the step." Hint: "Find your new distance from the mirror, then double it." Read: "You stand 1.2 m from a mirror, then step 0.4 m closer. How far away does your image look now?" Why: you are now 1.2 − 0.4 = 0.8 m in front of the mirror. Your image is 0.8 m behind it. So it looks 0.8 + 0.8 = 1.6 m away. The distance shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 10, show, Only where the light goes: the lamp, the mirror, its image and the eye. Words: "No light really comes from behind the mirror. So a screen put at the image would show nothing. The image is the same size as the object, and upright. But it is seen only by an eye that reflected light reaches. Past the mirror's end, no reflected ray arrives." Then "Drag the eye past the end of the mirror." Read: "With the eye past the end of the mirror, no reflected ray reaches it. A note says the image cannot be seen from here." Still: the eye past the mirror's end. Screen 11, do, Who sees it?: a short mirror on a wall with a lamp in front of it. A and B stand in front of the mirror. C stands to one side, close to the wall, past the mirror's end. "Which of them can see the lamp's image?" Choices, in a column: A and B (right); All three; Only C; Only B. Hint on All three: "Draw C's line to the image. It misses the mirror." Hint on Only C: "C sees the lamp itself. C's line to the image misses the mirror." Hint on Only B: "A's line to the image also crosses the mirror." Read: "A lamp stands in front of a short wall mirror. A and B stand in front of the mirror. C stands to one side, close to the wall, past its end. Which of them can see the lamp's image?" Why: an eye sees the image only if its straight line to the image crosses the mirror. Only then does reflected light reach it. A's and B's lines cross the mirror. C's line misses it. After Check each person's line to the image appears. Screen 12, show, Two mirrors: the switch turns on a second mirror at 45° below the first, making a periscope. Words: "This view is from the side. A mirror at 45° turns light through 90°. It arrives and leaves at 45° to the normal. Two such mirrors, one above the other, make a periscope. The second mirror makes an image of the first one's image. So the final image is as far away as the whole folded path." Then "Switch on the second mirror." Read: "Light travels 10 m from the lamp to the top mirror. It drops 1.5 m to the lower mirror, then travels 0.1 m to the eye. The image looks 10 + 1.5 + 0.1 = 11.6 m away." Still: the second mirror on. Screen 13, do, mixed, typed, The periscope: the periscope from screen 12 with its distances labelled and the folded path showing "?". "A periscope's mirrors are 2 m apart. An object is 30 m from the top mirror, and your eye is 0.1 m from the lower mirror. How far away does the object's image look?" A typed answer: 32.1 m, to one decimal place. Slips: 30 m, "That is only the first leg. The light still drops, then travels out to your eye."; 32 m, "Add the last 0.1 m, from the lower mirror to your eye."; 2.1 m, "Count the 30 m too. The image is as far as the whole path." Hint: "Add every leg of the folded path." Read: "A periscope's mirrors are 2 m apart. An object is 30 m from the top mirror, and your eye is 0.1 m from the lower mirror. How far away does the object's image look?" Why: the top mirror puts a first image 30 m behind it. That image is 30 + 2 = 32 m from the lower mirror. So the lower mirror puts the final image 32 m behind itself. Your eye is 0.1 m in front of that mirror. So the image looks 32 + 0.1 = 32.1 m away. The path shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 14, do, mixed, typed, A knocked mirror: the periscope's top mirror turned off 45°, with a small arc between it and its dashed 45° line. The knock is drawn larger than real, and a note says so. The picture shows the light it sends down leaning off vertical, its angle showing "?". "A periscope's top mirror is knocked 2° off its 45°. How far off vertical does it now send the light down?" A typed answer: 4°, a whole number. Slips: 2°, "The light turns twice as far as the mirror."; 1°, "Double the mirror's turn. Don't halve it." Hint: "Turning a mirror turns the reflected light twice as far." Read: "A periscope's top mirror is knocked 2° off its 45°. How far off vertical does it now send the light down?" Why: the light arriving is still level. Turning the mirror 2° changes the angle to the normal by 2° on the way in and 2° on the way out. So the light it sends down turns 2 × 2 = 4° off vertical. The angle shows "?" until the answer is checked.
interactive.ignores: The dashed lines behind the mirror show where rays seem to come from. No light travels along them. The picture is flat. It looks down from above, except the periscope screens, which look from the side. On the knocked-mirror screen the knock is drawn larger than real. The mirror is perfectly flat and sends back all the light that strikes it. A real mirror soaks up a little light. So its image is a little dimmer than the object. In a glass mirror the shiny layer sits behind the glass. The glass's front face adds a faint second reflection. The lamp and the eye are drawn as points. Real eyes come in pairs, and each pupil has some width. Curved mirrors are left out. They make images bigger or smaller. Light as a wave is left out too. Every distance and angle is an example figure.

explain.text:
A flat mirror sends light off at the same angle it arrives. Your eye then traces that light straight back. So you see the object's image behind the mirror, as far behind it as the object is in front.

Start with the angles. Light travels through air in straight lines, so draw it as rays. Where a ray strikes the mirror, draw a line at 90° to the surface. That line is the [[normal]]. Both angles are measured from it. The angle the ray arrives at is the angle of incidence. The angle it leaves at is the angle of reflection. The two are equal.[^1] That is the [[law of reflection]]. A ray 25° from the surface is 90 − 25 = 65° from the normal. So it leaves at 65° on the other side. Turn the mirror 10°, and the angle of incidence changes by 10°. So the angle of reflection changes by 10° too. The angle between the arriving and leaving rays is the two angles added. So it changes by 20°. Hold the arriving ray still, and the reflected ray turns twice as far as the mirror.

Now the image. Your eye cannot tell that light bounced. It judges where light comes from by tracing each ray straight back. Light from one point of an object spreads out. Each ray strikes the mirror at its own spot. The angles are equal, so each traced-back ray is the incoming ray flipped across the mirror's line. So every one passes through the same point, straight across the mirror from the object point. That point is the [[image]], as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.[^2] Stand 1.5 m in front of a mirror, and your image is 1.5 m behind it. So it is 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0 m from you. No light really comes from behind the mirror. So a screen put at the image would show nothing. The image is seen only by an eye that reflected light reaches. It is the same size as the object, and upright. A mirror at 45° to the light turns it through 90°. That is because the light arrives and leaves at 45° to the normal. Two such mirrors, one above the other, make a periscope. The second mirror makes an image of the first image. So the final image sits as far away as the whole folded path.

This is a simple model. It uses rays, a perfectly flat mirror and a point object. Real mirrors soak up a little light and are not perfectly flat. So real images are a little dimmer and softer. **A flat mirror sends light off at the angle it arrives, so its image sits as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.**

analogy.text: To bank a ball off a cushion into a pocket, you can aim at the pocket's mirror copy. That copy sits as far behind the cushion as the pocket is in front. A ball that rolls with no side spin leaves the cushion at about the angle it arrived at. So the straight line to the copy is the ball's real path, folded at the cushion. A mirror's image works the same way. The eye looks along the straight line to the image. The light really took that line, folded at the mirror.
analogy.breaks: A real ball leaves a cushion at only roughly its arriving angle. Spin, speed and the cushion's give all change it. Light off a flat, smooth mirror keeps the equal angles. A ball also takes just one path. Light spreads from every point of an object, so many rays meet at its image.

practice.text:
- Treat a mirror as a second source of any beam it can catch. Keep a laser's reflection out of everyone's eyes.
- Draw the mirror. Then draw the normal where the ray strikes.
- Measure both angles from the normal. If you are given the angle to the surface, take it away from 90°.
- To find an image, draw a line from the object square to the mirror. Carry it on as far again behind the mirror.
- To check who can see the image, draw a straight line from each eye to it. If the line crosses the mirror, that eye sees the image.
- With two mirrors, find the first image. Then treat it as the object for the second mirror.

**Rule of thumb:** turn a mirror, and its reflected beam turns twice as far. To move a reflected spot 10°, turn the mirror 10 ÷ 2 = 5°. Your own image looks twice as far from you as the mirror is.

**Worked example:** you use an inspection mirror to look for a loose cable behind a panel. The light travels 0.3 m from the cable to the mirror, then 0.4 m on to your eye. The image sits 0.3 m behind the mirror, along the line you look down. So the cable looks 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7 m away. It is as if its light came to you in a straight line.

**Common mistakes**
- Measuring the angles from the mirror's surface instead of the normal.
- Turning a mirror by the whole angle you want the beam to move.
- Putting the image on the mirror's surface, or on your line of sight to the object.
- Expecting the image to be seen from anywhere. Only an eye that reflected light reaches sees it.
- Counting only the first leg of a folded path.

interactive.html:
A flat mirror, with light drawn as straight rays. Every figure is an example.

Light leaves a mirror at the angle it arrives. The image is as far behind as the object is in front.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the ray to the eye meeting the mirror at equal angles, with its dashed line back always ending at the same image point, when you drag the eye along the bench.

checks.label: The law of reflection states that: angle of incidence = angle of reflection: for every torch angle from 25° to 65° and every turn of the mirror up to 20° either way, the beam leaves at the same angle to the normal as it arrives, and the Equal angles screen labels both 35°

The distance from the object to the mirror is the same as the distance from the mirror to the image: for lamps 15 to 65 cm in front, light from the lamp that bounces by the law into any eye has its traced-back line end at one point, as far behind the mirror as the lamp is in front; the image screen labels 40 cm and 40 cm

Turning the mirror turns the reflected beam twice as far: 10° turns it 20° while both angles to the turning normal go from 30° to 40°, the 15° answer turned by its handle puts the beam on the target's new spot 30° round, and a 45° mirror knocked 2° sends level light down 4° off vertical (drawn larger, 8° and 16°)
A mirror at 45° turns level light through 90°, so two of them, one above the other, send it out the way it came in; the folded paths add to 10 + 1.5 + 0.1 = 11.6 m and 30 + 2 + 0.1 = 32.1 m

Only an eye that reflected light reaches sees the image: the eye at the start of Only where the light goes sees it and the eye past the mirror's end does not; A and B see it, and C, past the end, does not

Each typed answer and slip is worked from the lesson's figures: 90 − 25 = 65° (25, 115); 30 ÷ 2 = 15° (30, 60); 0.8 + 0.8 = 1.6 m (2.0, 0.8, 2.4); 30 + 2 + 0.1 = 32.1 m (30, 32, 2.1); 2 × 2 = 4° (2, 1); each answer as printed is graded right and each slip wrong
Before Check nothing gives the answer away: no typed answer is drawn, the beam on Which way? has not left, and no ray or image is drawn on Find the image or Who sees it?
Every demonstration settles within 5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; the second mirror's motion and every answer's motion settle within 3 s

warnings: SVG labels "normal" and "45°" are only 2 px apart on one row, so they read as one: leave at least 4 px between them, or label only what differs (at step = step 12, and 1 more setting)

applied.problem: "Your own image is twice your distance from the mirror" reads, alone on a card, as if the image sat twice as far behind the mirror; it sits as far behind as you are in front, and only looks twice your distance away from you.
"A mirror at 45° turns light through 90°" is true only when the mirror is at 45° to the arriving light, as in a periscope; a mirror at 45° to something else can turn light by any angle.
A rolling ball always spins, so "rolls without spin" contradicts itself; the bank-shot aim needs no side spin, which is what the breaks already name.
